questions.source_definition: The source gives an explicit nonempty list of permutations of the same n vertices, n≥1. Its output is a tree realizing all orders as FIFO breadth-first traversals, with arbitrary neighbor tie orders, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: An explicitly listed nonempty profile of permutations must be realized by FIFO breadth-first search on one tree, with arbitrary neighbor tie orders. The target is an explicit Horn formula; its outputs are satisfying assignments or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: A polynomial reduction would give both recognition and tree construction for the remaining traversal-support case.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a finite ground set and an explicit family of subsets. A valid output assigns two colors so that every subset meets both colors, or reports NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target gives two binary rooted acyclic networks on the same uniquely labelled leaves and a bound k. Find a common contraction with at least k internal vertices, using acyclicity-preserving internal-edge contractions, or report NO-SOLUTION. A witness supplies both contraction sequences and their labelled isomorphism.
questions.board_importance: This isolates the difficulty of comparing evolutionary networks under a basic structural simplification.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a finite ground set and an explicit family of three-element subsets. A valid output assigns two colors so that every subset meets both colors, or reports NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target is a weakly connected binary acyclic network with exactly two roots. Find a spanning forest rooted at those roots, with the original leaves, such that every excluded edge joins different components, or report NO-SOLUTION. Roots have indegree/outdegree (0,2), internal vertices (1,2) or (2,1), and leaves (1,0).
questions.board_importance: The question separates easy spanning-forest existence from the constraints imposed by proper phylogenetic forest representations.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is a conjunction of clauses of three distinct unnegated variables. A valid assignment gives both truth values to every clause; an infeasible instance returns NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target is a connected bipartite graph of diameter at most five. A witness is a nontrivial vertex bipartition in which every vertex has exactly one neighbor across the cut; otherwise the output is NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: The diameter restriction targets a missing boundary in the structural complexity of perfect matching cuts.

questions.source_definition: The source is a connected bipartite graph of radius at most four. Its outputs are perfect matchings whose deletion disconnects the graph, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Both problems ask for a perfect matching whose deletion disconnects a connected bipartite graph, or NO-SOLUTION. The source radius is at most four and the target radius at most three.
questions.board_importance: This addresses a small-radius boundary for a matching that also acts as an edge separator.

questions.source_definition: The source is a connected bipartite graph of radius at most four. Its outputs are nontrivial cuts with crossing degree at most one, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Both problems ask for a nontrivial vertex bipartition with at most one opposite neighbor per vertex, or NO-SOLUTION. Inputs are connected bipartite graphs, with radius at most four in the source and at most three in the target.
questions.board_importance: The question asks whether one fewer distance layer crosses the tractability boundary for Matching Cut.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is a conjunction of clauses of three distinct unnegated variables. A valid assignment gives both truth values to every clause; an infeasible instance returns NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Source clauses contain three distinct unnegated variables and require both truth values in each clause. The target is a connected bipartite graph of radius at most three, with exactly one opposite neighbor at every vertex in a valid nontrivial cut.
questions.board_importance: This resolves a missing radius case between known tractable and hard regions.

questions.source_definition: The source is a connected simple graph of maximum degree at most four. Its outputs are nontrivial vertex bipartitions with at most one opposite neighbor per vertex, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The source is a connected simple graph of maximum degree four and asks for a nontrivial cut of crossing degree at most one. The target is connected, claw-free, of maximum degree six, and permits at most two opposite neighbors per vertex.
questions.board_importance: A result would determine the exact maximum-degree boundary for 2-Cut on claw-free graphs.

questions.source_definition: The source gives positive binary integer weights. A valid output is a subset whose sum is half the total, or NO-SOLUTION if no such subset exists.
questions.target_definition: On one machine, each job has a first operation of common length p, an exact delay p, a second operation of length b_i, and a deadline d_i. Binary integer start times must avoid overlap and meet every deadline; zero-length second operations are allowed.
questions.board_importance: A hardness result would isolate the effect of deadlines in a highly uniform coupled-task scheduling model.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target is a graph allowing parallel edges and loops. Degree-eight vertices require indegree in {1,4}; degree-two vertices require indegree in {0,2}. A solution orients every edge subject to these rules, without externally fixed ports.
questions.board_importance: This tests whether a small uniform orientation constraint can encode Boolean computation without supplied constants.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: Given a simple graph, represent each vertex by two disjoint unit intervals so that intersection is exactly adjacency and no point lies in more than three intervals, or report NO-SOLUTION. A finite endpoint encoding is required.
questions.board_importance: Depth three is a boundary between simpler representations and known harder cases in intersection-graph recognition.

questions.source_definition: The source is a connected graph of diameter at most four. Its outputs are nontrivial cuts having exactly one opposite neighbor at every vertex, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Both problems ask for a nontrivial bipartition with exactly one opposite neighbor per vertex, or NO-SOLUTION. The connected source graph has diameter at most four; the connected target graph has diameter at most three.
questions.board_importance: The question seeks the missing diameter boundary for Perfect Matching Cut.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target gives n distinct positive binary integers a_i and a sum σ, with sum_i(a_i+2i)=nσ. Find permutations b and c of [n] such that a_i+b_i+c_i=σ for every i, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: This asks whether arithmetic matching remains hard when two lists are fixed consecutive integers and the remaining list is distinct.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: Each target string is a sequence of finite sets of explicit words; concatenation defines its finite language. Find a word in the symmetric difference of the two languages, or report that the languages are equal. Nested language expressions are not allowed.
questions.board_importance: The question concerns the cost of comparing compact representations of uncertain strings.

questions.source_definition: The source asks whether a finite existential formula of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals is satisfiable, using binary integer coefficients. Recovery must respect the campaign’s finite algebraic witness representation; an unsatisfiable instance returns NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target asks whether a binary rational matrix has a rank-bounded approximation with unweighted entrywise L1 error strictly less than a rational ε. The strict inequality is part of the question; an accepted factor witness uses the specified finite rational encoding.
questions.board_importance: Real-algebraic hardness would strengthen ordinary NP-hardness and identify a deeper obstruction in robust low-rank fitting.

questions.target: Cycle factor containing an even cycle
questions.source_definition: The source gives a digraph and two designated terminal pairs. Its outputs are two vertex-disjoint directed paths joining the respective pairs, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The source asks for two vertex-disjoint directed paths between prescribed terminal pairs. The target is a loopless digraph and asks for a spanning directed cycle factor containing at least one even cycle; directed two-cycles are allowed.
questions.board_importance: This addresses the complexity difference between parity conditions imposed on some cycles and on all cycles of a factor.

questions.source_definition: The source gives positive binary integer weights. A valid output is a subset whose sum is half the total, or NO-SOLUTION if no such subset exists.
questions.target_definition: The target fixes the job order on three machines and permits varying operation patterns with positive integer processing times. Choose legal operation assignments meeting a makespan bound in the nonpreemptive blocking model, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: The question isolates assignment complexity after sequencing choices have been removed.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: Given a rational matrix M and separate integer widths p and q, find real factors U,V,W,Z with M=(UV)⊙(WZ), where UV has rank at most p and WZ rank at most q, or report NO-SOLUTION. Signs are unrestricted and witnesses use a common real algebraic primitive-element encoding.
questions.board_importance: Hadamard factorization is a compact matrix representation; this asks whether deciding exact representability is computationally hard.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: Given a nonempty rational matrix M and nonnegative integer budget b, find real A,B with M=A⊙B and rank(A)+rank(B)≤b, or report NO-SOLUTION. Witnesses encode both rank factorizations over one real algebraic primitive element; zero widths and either factor order are allowed.
questions.board_importance: This targets the total rank cost used to measure Hadamard representation size, rather than a preassigned allocation of ranks.

questions.source_definition: The source gives d≥1, an explicit binary activity array of length 2ᵈ defining T, and k≥0. Its outputs are subsets X⊆T of size at most k that dominate the cube graph induced by T, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target gives a hypercube dimension ℓ≥1 in unary, positive integer weighted ordered demands between distinct vertices, and a nonnegative integer K. A valid output is a partial matching whose demand-weighted shortest-route cost is at most K/2. Static edges cost 1, matching edges cost 1/2, and each route changes link medium at most twice. Every vertex has one switch port; there are no capacity or congestion constraints. Return NO-SOLUTION if no matching qualifies.
questions.board_importance: This asks whether allowing a second alternation changes the complexity of a tightly constrained reconfigurable network model.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: Given a graph G and alphabet budget k, find a vertex order, a letter for every vertex, and a directed decoder on at most k letters such that each earlier/later vertex pair is adjacent exactly when its ordered letter pair is in the decoder.
questions.board_importance: This addresses recognition when the alphabet is an input parameter, beyond fixed-alphabet structural results.

questions.source_definition: The source is a connected simple graph of maximum degree at most four. Its outputs are nontrivial vertex bipartitions with at most one opposite neighbor per vertex, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The source is a connected simple graph of maximum degree four and seeks a nontrivial cut of crossing degree at most one. The target is a connected line graph and seeks a nontrivial cut of crossing degree at most two.
questions.board_importance: The d=2 case tests a missing boundary for degree-bounded cuts on line graphs.

questions.source_definition: The source is a finite collection of labelled quartet trees. Its outputs are unrooted trees displaying every prescribed quartet, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The source asks for a tree displaying a collection of prescribed unrooted quartets. The target asks for a branch decomposition of a graph such that every cut has bipartite induced matching number at most one.
questions.board_importance: Width-one recognition concerns the simplest nontrivial level of a width measure used for graph algorithms.

questions.source: Height-one poset interval dimension at most three
questions.source_definition: The source is an explicitly encoded height-one poset. Its outputs are at most three interval orders whose intersection is that poset, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The fixed host has one a–b edge, three parallel b–c edges, and one c–d edge. Represent the target graph by connected subgraphs of a subdivision of this host, with intersection exactly adjacency and each pairwise set difference connected or empty.
questions.board_importance: This tests recognition on a small host where branching and non-crossing constraints interact.

questions.target: Nonnegative integer rank two for 3×3 matrices
questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: Given a 3×3 nonnegative integer matrix with binary-encoded entries of ordinary rank exactly two, find nonnegative integer U of size 3×2 and V of size 2×3 with M=UV, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: The question would distinguish arithmetic restrictions from real rank-two factorization in the smallest nontrivial matrix shape.

questions.source_definition: The source gives positive binary integer weights. A valid output is a subset whose sum is half the total, or NO-SOLUTION if no such subset exists.
questions.target_definition: The target gives independent coins with rational probabilities strictly between zero and one, positive test costs, and a rational bound K. Choose a fixed testing order whose expected cost is at most K, stopping at the first two different outcomes or after all coins.
questions.board_importance: Nonuniform costs remove a symmetry exploited in sequential testing and may change the complexity of choosing an order.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a rational symmetric matrix R with diagonal one. Its outputs are rational convex mixtures of sign vectors s∈{−1,+1}ⁿ realizing R as the weighted sum of ssᵀ, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target is a fully symmetric rational order-four tensor T of variable dimension with T[i,i,i,i]=T[i,i,j,j]=1 for every i,j. Ask for a representation as a sum of real fourth tensor powers, with no term-count bound. On this normalized domain the output encoding is a rational convex mixture of fourth powers of sign vectors, or NO-SOLUTION; equivalence of that certificate convention to real decomposability is part of the theorem.
questions.board_importance: The question connects a combinatorial marginal-consistency problem to a normalized polynomial representation.

questions.target: Normalized planar ReLU training with an error gap
questions.source_definition: A source instance has clauses of three unnegated variables. A valid assignment makes exactly one variable true in each clause; an infeasible instance returns NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target has rational two-dimensional data in [-1,1], a hidden-unit budget, signed output weights in {−1,+1}, and a rational squared-error threshold 0<τ≤1. The theorem must separate satisfiable from unsatisfiable sources by the stated error gap and give finite encoded accepted parameters.
questions.board_importance: This targets exact training complexity in two input dimensions under normalization, closer to a basic learning model than unrestricted constructions.

questions.source_definition: The source is Positive 1-in-3-SAT with explicit clauses of three unnegated variables. Its valid output is the correct YES/NO answer.
questions.target_definition: The target is a graph with no induced path on thirteen vertices and asks for a nontrivial cut having exactly one opposite neighbor at every vertex. The archived fixed theorem requests decision outputs; it does not establish witness extraction. Its valid output for this fixed theorem is the correct YES/NO answer.
questions.board_importance: The question addresses a forbidden-path boundary for perfect matching cuts.

questions.source_definition: The source is a connected graph containing no induced disjoint union of three edges. Its outputs are nontrivial cuts with crossing degree at most two, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Both endpoints are connected simple graphs and seek a nontrivial bipartition with at most two opposite neighbors per vertex. The source excludes three disjoint induced edges; the target excludes an induced six-vertex path.
questions.board_importance: Together with P5-free tractability, hardness here would identify an exact forbidden-path boundary.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a connected graph with no induced disjoint union of three three-vertex paths, and a bound k. Its outputs are nonempty matching cuts of size at most k, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Given a connected graph and integer k, ask for a nonempty matching cut of at most k edges, or NO-SOLUTION. The source excludes three disjoint induced three-vertex paths and the target excludes an induced nine-vertex path. This is a threshold problem, not an exact-optimum output contract.
questions.board_importance: The question refines the structural boundary for finding small matching separators.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a planar graph of maximum degree three and a bound k. Its outputs are independent vertex sets of size at least k, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Given a planar graph G and integer t, find at least t vertices M such that every radius-r ball contains at most r members of M for every vertex and every integer 1≤r≤the number of vertices, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: Multipacking links metric packing constraints to domination-type graph parameters; planar hardness would clarify how geometry affects its complexity.

questions.target: Dimension of a poset with a planar diagram
questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target supplies a finite poset, an upward planar Hasse diagram with rational polyline coordinates, and a dimension bound d. Find at most d linear orders whose intersection is the poset, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: This separates the complexity of order dimension from the complexity of obtaining a planar drawing.

questions.target: Plane cubic augmentation allowing new vertices
questions.source_definition: The source gives a fixed plane graph. Its outputs are three-connected cubic augmentations adding only edges while extending the embedding, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target is a fixed plane graph and asks for a three-connected cubic supergraph extending its embedding, allowing additional vertices and edges. The source version permits only additional edges. Valid augmentations require a finite combinatorial embedding encoding.
questions.board_importance: Allowing new vertices changes the feasible extensions and is not automatically covered by edge-only augmentation hardness.

questions.source: Strongly consistent ordering with a given partition
questions.target: Proper thinness with an input class budget
questions.source_definition: The source gives a graph and a vertex partition. Its outputs are orders for which both the order and its reverse are consistent with the partition: if u<v<w, u and v share a class, and uw is an edge, then vw is an edge. Otherwise return NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The source supplies a graph and vertex partition and asks for an order strongly consistent in both directions. The target supplies only a graph and a class budget, and asks for both a partition within that budget and such an order.
questions.board_importance: The question isolates the complexity contributed by choosing the partition in an ordering-based graph representation.

questions.source_definition: The starting point is 3-SAT: given a Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause, decide whether a satisfying assignment exists.
questions.target_definition: The target instance consists of an m × n nonnegative rational matrix X and a nonnegative rational threshold τ, both encoded in binary. It asks whether nonnegative real matrices W of size m × 2 and H of size 2 × n satisfy the error bound below. The factors may be asymmetric and need not have rational entries.
questions.board_importance: Nonnegative matrix factorization represents nonnegative data using a small number of nonnegative components. Fixing that number to two gives the first nontrivial approximation case. Establishing hardness here would show that even this small model can resist polynomial-time exact global optimization.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a simple bipartite graph and, for every vertex, an explicit list contained in {1,2,3}. Its outputs are proper colorings respecting all lists, or NO-SOLUTION; empty lists are allowed.
questions.target_definition: The target gives a finite simple bipartite graph H with an ordered partition into seven nonempty connected vertex sets. The first six are singleton bundles of weights 4096, 1024, 256, 64, 16 and 4; the seventh has weight 1. A valid output is a proper coloring by positive integers for which the sum, over bundles, of weight times maximum color is at most 5823, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: This tests the effect of connectivity requirements on a small fixed collection of coloring bundles.

questions.source_definition: The source asks whether a finite existential formula of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals is satisfiable, using binary integer coefficients. Recovery must respect the campaign’s finite algebraic witness representation; an unsatisfiable instance returns NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Given a simple graph and layer budget k, find a straight-line drawing and an edge partition into at most k crossing-free layers, or report NO-SOLUTION. Coordinates require a finite real-algebraic encoding.
questions.board_importance: Real-algebraic hardness would explain geometric recognition difficulty beyond ordinary combinatorial NP-hardness.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target is a graph alone, with no boundary order or holes supplied. A positive output must encode a simple polygon whose vertex visibility graph is exactly the input. The precise finite coordinate model remains to be fixed.
questions.board_importance: Visibility recognition is a central inverse problem in computational geometry: reconstruct geometry from pairwise visibility information.

questions.target: Proper star colouring on split graphs
questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target gives a split graph and color budget k. Find a proper coloring with at most k colors in which no four-vertex path is bichromatic, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: The restriction asks how much complexity survives when the graph decomposes into a clique and an independent set.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a simple graph. Its outputs are partitions of its vertices into triples each inducing a triangle, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target has symmetric pair values in {0,1,2} and asks for a partition into triples with no justified envy. An agent envies replacing another when its utility improves and both remaining members strictly prefer the incoming agent.
questions.board_importance: This isolates existence complexity in a small-valued symmetric coalition model.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a simple graph and an integer threshold. Its outputs are independent sets of at least that size, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target gives goods with a conflict graph and identical nonnegative rational additive values for three agents. Find three disjoint independent bundles forming an EF1 partial allocation that is maximal under adding any single unallocated good to any bundle.
questions.board_importance: This tests whether fairness remains algorithmically accessible when feasibility conflicts and maximality interact, even for three identical agents.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target gives a precedence DAG of unit-time jobs and an integer deadline T. Find an integer-slot schedule on three identical machines respecting precedences and finishing by T, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: This is a longstanding small-machine scheduling boundary with broad relevance to precedence-constrained computation.

questions.source_definition: The source gives an even number of positive binary integer weights. A valid subset contains exactly half the weights and has half their total sum; otherwise the output is NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The source asks for half the input weights with half their total sum. The target has three job types in high-multiplicity encoding, positive integer processing times on unrelated machines, and a makespan bound. An output is an integer assignment-count matrix.
questions.board_importance: The question asks whether a fixed number of job types suffices for exact scheduling tractability under compressed multiplicities.

questions.source_definition: The source gives task deadlines. Its outputs are finite schedules visiting each task exactly twice, meeting first-visit and successive-gap deadlines with no final-tail condition, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: A k-Visits solution is a finite word containing each task exactly k times, with its first visit and every successive same-task gap bounded by the task deadline. There is no final-tail constraint. The source has k=2 and the target k=3.
questions.board_importance: The question isolates the effect of adding one required visit in a recurring scheduling model.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target gives a graph and a sequence of colored stacks. Each move places the next stack on an empty vertex; if it has a same-color neighbor, the new stack and its same-color neighbors clear. The goal is to place every stack, not to clear the final board.
questions.board_importance: This asks whether the lowest nontrivial clearing threshold already supports computational hardness.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: Tiles carry finite feature sets. Consecutive chosen tiles must share a currently present feature; moving deletes their common features. The goal is to remove all features, with no teleport or zero-effect moves.
questions.board_importance: Removing teleportation tests whether local feature transitions alone create hardness in the puzzle model.

questions.source_definition: The source gives positive binary integer weights. A valid output is a subset whose sum is half the total, or NO-SOLUTION if no such subset exists.
questions.target_definition: The target allows a variable job order. Each job has a mandatory first operation on machine one, flexible intermediate operations, and a final operation on machine two, with positive processing times, no buffer, and no overtaking. Seek an order and legal splits meeting the deadline.
questions.board_importance: The question asks whether assignment flexibility causes hardness even with just two machines.

questions.source_definition: The source is a connected graph containing no induced disjoint union of three edges. Its outputs are nontrivial cuts with crossing degree at most two, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Both problems seek a nontrivial cut with at most two opposite neighbors per vertex in a connected simple graph. The source is 3P2-free and the target has no induced disjoint union of two four-vertex paths.
questions.board_importance: This addresses a remaining forbidden-induced-subgraph case for bounded-degree cuts.

questions.source_definition: The source gives a simple graph. Its outputs are vertex orders with no nested pair of independent edges, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: A queue layout consists of a vertex order and a partition of edges into queues, with no two independent edges nested within a queue. The source permits one queue and the target permits two; outputs include the order and queue assignment.
questions.board_importance: This asks whether recognizing the next queue level inherits the difficulty of one-queue recognition.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target must be a 2-tree and asks for a vertex order with one stack and one queue. Independent stack edges may not alternate and independent queue edges may not nest. A 2-tree starts from an edge and repeatedly adds a vertex adjacent to both endpoints of an existing edge.
questions.board_importance: The question asks whether choosing a mixed layout is hard even on a narrowly structured graph class.

questions.source_definition: A source instance is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula with at most three literals per clause. Its outputs are satisfying Boolean assignments, or NO-SOLUTION when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.target_definition: The target supplies rational planar centers; vertices are adjacent exactly when their squared distance is at most one. Find three colors such that every monochromatic induced graph is a disjoint union of cliques, or report NO-SOLUTION.
questions.board_importance: The question combines geometric restrictions with a coloring rule that permits monochromatic cliques, beyond ordinary proper coloring.

questions.target: Interval k-graph recognition without a partition
questions.source_definition: The source gives a simple graph. Its outputs are proper vertex colorings with at most three colors, or NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: The target gives a graph and k. Find at most k vertex classes and one closed interval per vertex so that adjacency holds exactly for intersecting intervals in different classes, or report NO-SOLUTION. Endpoint weak-order ranks give a finite encoding.
questions.board_importance: This isolates the difference between recognizing a representation with supplied classes and discovering the classes.

questions.source_definition: A Boolean CNF formula with three literals per clause is given explicitly. Return a satisfying truth assignment. Return NO-SOLUTION exactly when no such witness exists. Graphs, families and strings are explicit; numerical parameters use binary encodings.
questions.target_definition: Given a binary matrix and K, return at most K axis-aligned rectangles with integer row and column endpoints whose union is exactly the matrix's one entries. A valid output is a witness satisfying these conditions, or NO-SOLUTION exactly when none exists.
questions.board_importance: The task reconstructs a usable hardness rule for lossless rectangle-based representation of binary images.

questions.source_definition: Given a finite simple graph and k, return a vertex cover of size at most k, or NO-SOLUTION. All finite combinatorial structures are explicit and numerical data use binary encoding.
questions.target_definition: Given a finite string s, pointer cost h and budget B, return a dictionary D and compressed string C composed of literals and pointers to substrings of D. Recursive replacement must terminate and expand C to s. Count every literal as one unit and every pointer occurrence as h units across both D and C; require total cost at most B. Encode pointer destinations and substring endpoints explicitly.
questions.board_importance: This reconstructs a rule for selecting reusable dictionary phrases under an explicit storage-cost model.

questions.source_definition: Given a finite simple undirected graph and a nonnegative integer k, return a vertex set of size at most k meeting every edge. Return NO-SOLUTION exactly when no such witness exists. Graphs, families and strings are explicit; numerical parameters use binary encodings.
questions.target_definition: Given an explicit family C of subsets of a finite universe and K, return at most K basis subsets such that every member of C is the union of some of the basis subsets. A valid output is a witness satisfying these conditions, or NO-SOLUTION exactly when none exists.
questions.board_importance: A reconstructed rule connects covering to reusable set representations and Boolean data decomposition.

questions.source: Common stable matching with two changed agents on each side
questions.source_definition: The input gives the same n workers and n firms with two complete strict preference profiles A and B; at most two workers and at most two firms change their lists between profiles. An output is a perfect matching stable in both profiles, or NO-SOLUTION exactly when none exists.
questions.target_definition: The input is an explicit 2-CNF formula. A valid output is a satisfying truth assignment, or NO-SOLUTION exactly when the formula is unsatisfiable.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: a successful structured encoding would settle the first unresolved case after one-sided preference changes and could support robust market design when a few participants revise rankings. It would not classify arbitrary numbers of changed agents.

questions.target: Minimum-cost time-feasible reconciliation with host switches of distance at most three
questions.source_definition: An explicitly encoded Boolean 3-CNF formula is given. The valid output is YES if it has a satisfying assignment and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: The input contains two explicitly encoded rooted full binary host and parasite trees, a map from parasite leaves to host leaves, nonnegative binary-encoded event costs, and a binary-encoded cost bound K. The answer is YES exactly when a reconciliation mapping parasite vertices to host vertices respects the given leaves and the cospeciation, duplication and switch event rules of Antony, Martino and Sinaimeri, every host switch spans at most three host-tree edges, the temporal constraint digraph is acyclic, and total event cost is at most K; otherwise NO.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: hardness at distance three would locate the first possible boundary for biologically constrained reconciliation and help explain when exact host-switch reconstruction requires exponential search. It would not classify all fixed distances.

questions.target: Allowed-centers min-sum-radii on unweighted graph metrics
questions.source_definition: An explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula is given, with YES if satisfiable and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: An explicitly encoded connected simple unweighted graph G, a nonempty set A of allowed center vertices, integers k and D in binary are given. The answer is YES exactly when at most k pairs (center c in A, nonnegative integer radius r) cover every vertex within its graph distance from some chosen center and the sum of radii is at most D; otherwise NO. Zero-radius singleton clusters are allowed.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: classical hardness would finish the basic complexity picture for a natural facility-location restriction and clarify the effect of admissible sites. The result would not settle unrestricted unweighted MSR, for which a randomized quasipolynomial algorithm is known.

questions.target: Plane oriented geometric spanner with bounded dilation
questions.source_definition: An explicit planar Boolean 3-CNF instance, including its planar variable-clause incidence embedding, is given. Output YES if satisfiable and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: The input is a finite set of pairwise distinct rational-coordinate plane points and a positive rational threshold t, all in binary. The output is YES exactly when some simple strongly connected orientation of a plane straight-line graph on these points has oriented dilation at most t: for each point pair, the shortest directed closed walk through both has length at most t times the shortest triangle through them in the complete Euclidean graph. Otherwise output NO.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: the result would settle the hardness side of a natural directed geometric-network design problem relevant to sparse routing and motion-planning roadmaps. It would not resolve the separate undirected minimum-dilation triangulation question.

questions.source: Interval-graph subcoloring with an input color budget
questions.source_definition: An interval graph is given by an explicit list of rational closed intervals and a binary-encoded positive integer k. A valid output partitions the intervals into at most k classes such that the intersection graph induced by each class is a disjoint union of cliques, equivalently has no induced three-vertex path; output NO-SOLUTION exactly when no such partition exists.
questions.target_definition: An explicit directed network with integer capacities, integer costs and specified supplies and demands is given. A valid output is any minimum-cost integral feasible flow, or INFEASIBLE exactly when no feasible flow exists. All numbers are binary encoded.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: the result would settle a 2002 question that the 2025 subcoloring paper still lists as open and could yield exact channel or interval-resource grouping. It would not resolve subcoloring of general co-comparability graphs.

questions.target: Product Knapsack with unary profits and binary weights
questions.source_definition: The input is a list of positive binary-encoded integers a_i and a binary target T. Output YES exactly when some subset sums to T, and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: The input is a list of items with positive integer weights written in binary and positive integer profits written in unary, plus binary-encoded capacity C and product threshold V. Output YES exactly when some subset has total weight at most C and product of its profits at least V; otherwise NO.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: hardness would settle a natural encoding boundary in multiplicative knapsack and could transfer to tournament-bribery models through the published Product Knapsack connection, provided their probability restrictions match. It would not alone prove every such bribery variant hard.

questions.target: Two-subcoloring of height-one unit disk graphs
questions.source_definition: An explicit planar Boolean 3-CNF formula with a planar variable-clause incidence embedding is given. Output YES if satisfiable and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: The input is the adjacency list of a simple graph promised to have a representation by diameter-one closed disks whose centers lie in a horizontal strip of height at most one. Output YES exactly when its vertices can be partitioned into two classes, each inducing a disjoint union of cliques, equivalently containing no induced three-vertex path; otherwise NO. The reduction must produce a rational-coordinate representation to establish the promise, although the target input is the graph.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: hardness would close the geometric boundary left after bounded-height hardness and affect exact two-channel grouping in narrow wireless deployments. A polynomial algorithm would instead imply the paper's proposed 2-approximation route, but is not the requested positive reduction.

questions.target: Reachability in priority-inhibited unimolecular reaction networks
questions.source_definition: An explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula is given. Output YES exactly when it is satisfiable, and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: The input lists an ordered finite set of species, explicit reactions each converting exactly one molecule of one species to one of another species, an integer priority p between zero and the species count for each reaction, and binary-encoded start and target molecule-count vectors. A reaction with priority p is enabled only when its reactant is present and each of the first p species has count zero. Output YES exactly when a finite enabled reaction sequence reaches the target vector, and NO otherwise.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: hardness would separate priority inhibition from ordinary unimolecular reaction reachability and sharpen a basic model of biochemical computation. It would not give the exact class if the priority problem is harder than NP.

questions.target: Two-machine preemptive unit-job in-tree scheduling with release dates and total completion bound
questions.source_definition: An explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula is given, with YES if satisfiable and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: The input is a finite set of unit-processing-time jobs, nonnegative integer release times, in-tree precedence arcs (each job has at most one successor), and an integer bound B, all explicitly or in binary as appropriate. Preemption is allowed on two identical processors, but a job cannot run on both simultaneously. Output YES exactly when some feasible schedule respects releases and precedence and has sum of completion times at most B; otherwise NO.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: hardness would resolve a classical two-processor boundary for minimizing mean completion time under task dependencies. It would not follow merely from hardness when the number of processors is part of the input.

questions.target: Iterated weak-dominance solvability of two-action anonymous games
questions.source_definition: An explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula is given, with YES if satisfiable and NO otherwise.
questions.target_definition: An explicit n-player anonymous game is given. Each player has two actions, and the input lists that player's integer payoff for each own action and each count from zero to n-1 of other players choosing action one. Output YES exactly when some sequence of deleting weakly dominated actions from the current reduced game leaves exactly one action for every player; otherwise NO. Weak dominance requires never lower payoff and a strict improvement for some remaining opponents' action profile. With two actions, dominance by a mixed strategy is equivalent to dominance by the other pure action.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: hardness would close the two-action boundary between tractable symmetric anonymous games and known three-action hardness, with relevance to strategic simplification in large anonymous populations. It would not classify other equilibrium concepts.

questions.source_definition: Input is an explicitly listed undirected graph, three distinct terminals, and an integer budget k. The output is YES exactly when at most k edges disconnect every pair of terminals; otherwise NO. All integers use binary encoding.
questions.target_definition: Input is an explicitly listed undirected graph H, distinct s,t, a designated edge b, and a binary budget K. Output YES exactly when deleting at most K edges other than b leaves at least one s–t path and makes every remaining s–t path use b; otherwise NO. The surviving-path requirement excludes a vacuous cut.
questions.board_importance: High: it would settle the hardness side of the P-versus-NP-hard classification explicitly left open for general undirected Network Diversion, with direct interpretation for forced bottlenecks in transportation and communication networks.

questions.source_definition: Input is an explicitly listed undirected graph, three distinct terminals, and a binary edge-deletion budget k. Output YES exactly if deleting at most k edges disconnects every terminal pair; otherwise NO.
questions.target_definition: Input is an explicitly listed undirected temporal graph with timestamped edge appearances, s,z, a deadline ℓ and edge-deletion budget K, all integers binary. Output YES exactly if deleting at most K temporal edge appearances eliminates every simple s–z path with strictly increasing timestamps and duration last-minus-first-plus-one at most ℓ; otherwise NO. ℓ is part of the input and may exceed two.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: this would close the precise strict-versus-nonstrict gap in temporal network interdiction with deadlines, distinguishing it from already polynomial unrestricted strict temporal cut and already hard non-strict deadline cut.

questions.source_definition: Input is an explicitly listed undirected graph G. Output YES exactly if some total order of V(G) orients each edge forward so that every directed path in the resulting orientation has at most two edges; otherwise NO. This is the 2-Orientability problem in ICDT 2026, Proposition 11, equivalent to 3-colorability via Gallai–Roy–Vitaver. It is not the unrelated indegree-bounded orientation problem.
questions.target_definition: Input is a finite collection of read/write operation sequences on named objects and binary span bound K. Each operation has unit duration; per-transaction order is strict; conflicting operations on the same object cannot be simultaneous; the conflict-precedence graph must be acyclic. At most two objects are contention points. A schedule may be shifted so its first operation occurs at time zero, and its span is last occupied time plus one. Output YES if such a schedule has span at most K, otherwise NO.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: this would move the known database scheduling hardness boundary from unrestricted contention to two objects, completing one side of the gap next to the one-contention-point polynomial algorithm.

questions.source_definition: Input is a unary-encoded multiset of positive item sizes, unary bin capacity B, and a binary or unary bin count m. Output YES exactly if all items fit in at most m bins of capacity B; otherwise NO. Use the standard strong-hardness family with total instance size polynomial in the unary quantities.
questions.target_definition: Input is a finite horizon, unary-encoded nonnegative energy forecast F(t), and unit-length jobs with unary energy demand e_j and release/deadline windows permitting at most two consecutive start times. No battery and no external energy are allowed. Output YES if each job can be assigned a legal slot and total demand in each slot does not exceed F(t); otherwise NO. The horizon is explicitly represented.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: this would settle the strong-hardness side of the weak-versus-strong boundary posed by the energy-autarky paper for its most restricted flexible jobs, informing when pseudo-polynomial scheduling is possible.

questions.source: Exact Fair Correlation Clustering on a Path with Ratio 1:c
questions.source_definition: Input is an explicitly listed path whose vertices are colored red or blue with |blue|=c|red| for an input integer c≥2. Positive pairs are path edges and all other pairs are negative. A valid output is any partition into clusters each containing red:blue in ratio 1:c that minimizes the number of positive pairs separated plus negative pairs kept together; if no fair partition exists, output NO-SOLUTION.
questions.target_definition: Input is a directed network with integral capacities and binary rational costs plus supplies and demands. Valid outputs are all integral feasible flows of minimum total cost, or NO-SOLUTION if infeasible.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: it would settle a path case explicitly left open in fair correlation clustering, beyond fixed fairlet-size algorithms, and give an exact algorithm for group-balanced clustering on sparse networks.

questions.source: EF1 + MMS + Pareto-Optimal Service Allocation on a Path
questions.source_definition: Input is an unweighted path with one hub, n identical agents, m−1≥n task vertices, and positive binary rational travel and service costs c_d,c_t. For a bundle S, cost is 2c_d(max(R(S),h)−min(L(S),h))+c_t|S|, with cost zero for empty S. Outputs are all complete allocations satisfying chores-EF1 (each nonempty own bundle can lose one task to cost no more than another bundle), cost at most the minimax-share threshold for every agent, and Pareto optimality; output NO-SOLUTION if none exists.
questions.target_definition: Input is a directed network with integral capacities, binary rational arc costs, and supplies/demands. Outputs are all integral feasible flows of minimum total cost, or NO-SOLUTION when infeasible.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: it would settle the combined fairness/efficiency case left open for two-dimensional path service costs, with a concrete allocation algorithm for delivery or field-service work.

questions.source_definition: Input is a unary-encoded 3-Partition instance with 3m positive integers of total mB and each strictly between B/4 and B/2. Output YES exactly when they split into m triples of sum B; otherwise NO.
questions.target_definition: Input is an explicitly listed bidirected compatibility graph, positive binary rational arc weights such that each reciprocal pair has equal arc weights and the resulting undirected edge totals take at most two distinct values, a partition of vertices into countries of size at most two, a rational target utility vector x, and rational deviation bound D. Country utility is the sum of weights of incoming matched arcs at its vertices. Output YES exactly if some maximum-total-edge-weight matching has max-country absolute deviation from x at most D; otherwise NO.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: it would locate a sharp fairness-complexity boundary in country-partitioned two-way kidney exchange where matching itself is polynomial but choosing an optimally fair maximum-weight matching may not be.

questions.source: Minimum-Weight Exact Red–Blue Bipartite Perfect Matching
questions.source_definition: Input is an explicitly listed bipartite graph with equal left and right vertex counts, red/blue edge colors, binary nonnegative integer edge weights, and binary k. Outputs are all perfect matchings containing exactly k red edges and having minimum total weight among those, or NO-SOLUTION if none exists.
questions.target_definition: Input is a directed network with integral capacities, binary rational costs and node balances. Outputs are all integral feasible flows of minimum total cost, or NO-SOLUTION if infeasible.
questions.board_importance: High: the 2026 assignment paper shows this problem subsumes several upgraded assignment and scheduling extensions. A positive reduction would also settle deterministic exact-color matching on bipartite graphs.

questions.source_definition: Input is a unary-encoded multiset A of positive integers, an integer q, and threshold T. Output YES exactly if A can be partitioned into q parts with the sum of squared part sums at most T; otherwise NO.
questions.target_definition: Input is an explicitly listed bidirected tree, a positive integer period Δ, and a binary threshold K. Assign each directed arc independently one residue in {0,…,Δ−1}, repeated every Δ time units. For every ordered vertex pair, use its unique directed path and the fastest strictly increasing traversal; sum duration minus static path length. Output YES if some arc labeling gives total excess time at most K, otherwise NO.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: it would classify the directed analogue of a recent temporal-network design problem, relevant when two directions of a transit link have separate departure phases.

questions.source_definition: Input is an n-by-n matrix of nonnegative binary rational utilities with zero diagonal. For coalition S, v(S) is the maximum total utility of a permutation of S, where fixed points represent zero-value dummy assignments. The output is the unique rational efficient and individually rational payoff vector that lexicographically minimizes the nonincreasing list of coalition excesses v(S)−x(S). There is no NO-SOLUTION case.
questions.target_definition: Input is an explicitly listed rational linear program with polynomially encoded coefficients. Valid outputs are all optimal rational solutions, or NO-SOLUTION when infeasible or unbounded. For this reduction every constructed instance must have an optimum.
questions.board_importance: Moderate: the nucleolus is an established fairness rule in cooperative exchange; a positive result would extend efficient computation beyond the known cyclic permutation-game subclass and apply to unbounded-cycle kidney exchange models.
